1.notes:
A strange seed is planted on its back at birth, and the plant sprouts and grows together with the creature. It drowses in bright sun, and the seed drinks the light to feed them both.
After a long rest in the sun it grows visibly stouter, and keepers judge its health by the freshness of the bulb.
1.scribe: The first entry of the old ledgers, and a gentle companion for a new keeper.

2.notes:
The bulb has swollen into a heavy bud, and the weight of it settles the creature onto four sure legs. A sweet scent from the bud is taken as a sign that the great flower is near to blooming.
It is often found resting in open meadows, gathering the sun that the bud demands.

3.notes:
The flower on its back opens fully when it draws in the sun, and it keeps to the move in search of open light. Its scent is said to soothe all quarrels nearby.
In the warm months it grows notably stronger, for the great blossom turns summer light into vigor.

4.notes:
A small lizard that plainly favors hot places. The flame at the tip of its tail burns with its life force, bright when it is healthy and thin when it is weary.
When rain falls, travelers report steam rising from the tail tip, and a careful keeper shelters it well.

5.notes:
Grown fierce and barbarous, it whips its burning tail about in battle and slashes with sharp claws. The heat of the swung flame is said to become nearly unbearable at close quarters.
It seeks out strong foes of its own accord, and calms only when it has won.

6.notes:
On broad wings it hunts for worthy opponents, and its inner fire burns hotter for every hard battle it survives. It breathes flame that melts stone, though it is said never to turn that fire on a weaker foe.
When its fury peaks, the flame at its tail flares a pale whitish blue, and the wise keep their distance.

7.notes:
Soon after birth its back swells and hardens into a shell, resilient enough to spring back when poked. It sprays foam from its mouth with surprising force.
The rounded shell serves it doubly, for it withdraws inside to weather blows, and its smooth curve lets the little turtle swim swiftly.

8.notes:
It hides in water to stalk unwary prey, and steers with its furred ears and tail to keep its balance at speed. The tail is prized as a mark of age and wisdom.
Old records hold that a Wartortle may live a very long life, and the scars upon its shell are read like a chronicle.

9.notes:
A heavy and deliberate beast bearing water cannons upon its shell, which fire jets said to punch through thick steel. It plants its great weight and does not yield ground.
It withdraws into the shell only at utmost need, trusting first to the pressure of its guns.

10.notes:
Its short feet are tipped with suction pads, so it climbs slopes, walls, and trees without tiring as it forages. Its whole body is given to eating leaves.
The horn upon its head releases a fierce odor when the creature is pressed, which drives off many a hungry bird.

11.notes:
Within this cocoon the flesh is soft and tender, and so the creature hardens its shell with all its small strength and waits. It can do little else but harden.
Though it seems a mere husk, the body within is busily preparing its wings, and patience is rewarded within days.

12.notes:
In battle it beats its wings at great speed to shed a toxic dust upon the air. A water-shedding powder coats the wings, so it gathers honey even in heavy rain.
It knows the blooming meadows well, and keepers follow it in flower season to find honey of their own.

13.notes:
It is found in forests eating leaves, most often beneath the very leaves it feeds upon. Upon its head sits a sharp barb of poison the length of a thumb.
Its sting is painful but rarely grave, and the barb is its only answer to every threat.

14.notes:
Nearly incapable of motion, it can only harden its shell against predators and endure. From this form it grows toward its adult shape while the outer casing stiffens.
It is sometimes found hanging thickly from tree boughs, still as fruit, waiting out its change.

15.notes:
It flies at high speed and strikes with the venomous stingers of its forelegs and tail, and of its three barbs the one at the tail carries the strongest poison. It answers any disturbance of its nest in furious numbers.
Travelers are counseled to pass the deep woods quietly, for a single angered scout summons the swarm.

16.notes:
A common sight in woods and on grassy roads, docile of temper and disinclined to fight. Threatened, it flaps at ground level to kick up blinding sand and makes its escape.
It is often the first wild creature a young keeper ever meets, and is fondly remembered for it.

17.notes:
Fiercely protective of its wide territory, it pecks without mercy at any intruder. It pins its prey with well grown claws and can carry it a great distance to the nest.
It circles its hunting grounds slowly, and farmers read its flight to know their fields are watched.

18.notes:
It spreads beautiful, broad wings to awe its enemies, and in a stoop it is said to reach a speed near twice that of sound. When hunting it skims low over water to pluck up unwary fish.
The gloss of its feathers has drawn admirers for generations, and many keepers raise it for splendor alone.

19.notes:
It lives wherever food is found and scavenges the whole day through. Its fangs grow without cease, and so it gnaws whatever lies at hand to pare them down.
It breeds quickly wherever it settles, and a single granary may keep a whole colony fed.

20.notes:
It steadies itself with its whiskers and is said to slow if ever they are cut. The teeth are stout enough to gnaw through cinder walls and thick planks.
Its webbed hind feet make it a fair swimmer, and it crosses rivers that would stop lesser vermin.

21.notes:
It eats bugs in grassy country and must beat its short wings at great speed merely to stay aloft. Its cry is loud and carries far.
Quarrelsome beyond its size, it defends its ground against far larger birds, and its shriek warns the whole flock of danger.

22.notes:
On huge and magnificent wings it can ride the air all day without once alighting. With its long thin beak it plucks small creatures from soil and shallow water.
It remembers an injury long, and the old tales say a wronged Fearow pursues its enemy across the whole of the land.

23.notes:
It moves without sound through the grass and swallows the eggs of small birds whole. The newly born carry no venom, and their bite is painful but harmless.
It sheds its skin as it grows, and country folk nail the cast-off skins above doorways for luck.

24.notes:
The fierce markings upon its belly are said to differ from country to country, and scholars sort them into many patterns. It flattens its hood to seem larger than it is.
Once it marks its prey it does not give up the chase, for its nature is patient and vengeful alike.

25.notes:
It stores lightning in the pouches of its cheeks, and when many gather their charge may call down storms upon the fields. It raises its tail to read its surroundings, and now and then the tail is struck for its trouble.
For all that, it is a warm and companionable creature, and no beast in Kanto is better loved.

26.notes:
Its long tail roots into the ground to spare the creature its own high voltage, which may reach ten thousand volts when the cheek pouches are full. Both ears stand straight when it is fully charged.
It glows faintly in the dark, and a keeper learns to judge its temper by the crackle of its fur.

27.notes:
It burrows deep in dry country far from water and comes up only to hunt. Its hide is tough and dry, and it rolls itself into a tight ball in an instant when threatened.
It bathes in sand as other beasts bathe in water, and its burrows honeycomb the desert hills.

28.notes:
When threatened it curls into a ball of spines, and thus curled it may roll at its foe or away to safety. It digs at an astonishing pace when it must.
Its claws and spikes snap off in hard digging and grow back within the day, and shed spikes litter its diggings like fallen thorns.

29.notes:
Though small and not quarrelsome, her venomous barbs make her a dangerous catch, and she will torment a persistent foe with poison spikes. Her horn is smaller than the male's.
She keeps to the company of her kin, and her whiskered ears are ever turned toward danger.

30.notes:
Of a calm and caring nature, her horn grows slowly and she prefers claw and tooth to its point. She chews food small for the young of her nest.
When her young are threatened her mildness ends at once, and few beasts fight harder.

31.notes:
Her hard scales are proof against most blows, and she uses her hefty bulk to deliver moves of great power. She seals the mouth of her nest with her own body to guard her young.
The old keepers say her strength is fiercest in defense, for she fights best with something behind her.

32.notes:
He stiffens his great ears to catch the least sound of danger, and he will strike first when he senses it. The larger his horn, the stronger the venom it holds.
He tests the wind constantly, and his temper is quick but honest.

33.notes:
An aggressive creature, quick to anger and quicker to charge, he stabs with his horn to drive a strong venom home. His hide has hardened into rough plates.
He scrapes his horn on stone to keep it keen, and the scored boulders mark his territory.

34.notes:
His tail is thick and terrible, and with it he smashes, constricts, and breaks whatever he seizes. One swing is said to topple a metal transmission tower.
Yet under a trusted keeper he grows calm, and the old drill kings are counted among the most loyal beasts of the kingdom.

35.notes:
A rare fairy of the mountains, its charm and its cry have won it many admirers, though it is seldom found. It is said to dance in rings under the full moon.
On quiet nights the mountain folk climb to watch the dancing from afar, and count it the best of omens.

36.notes:
A timid fairy, rarely seen, that runs and hides the moment it senses people. Its sensitive ears hear a pin drop a half mile off, and so it keeps to quiet places.
It is said to walk on the surface of still water on moonlit nights, and those few who have seen it never forget it.

37.notes:
At birth it bears a single white tail, which splits from the tip into six as it grows and is groomed. Inside its body burns a flame that never goes out.
When threatened by a stronger foe it feigns injury and slips away, for its cunning outweighs its size.

38.notes:
Very intelligent and very vengeful, it is said that the grasping of one of its nine tails may earn a curse of a thousand years. The tails hold a strange power, and its eyes see through to the heart.
It is written that this creature may live a thousand years, and the oldest are treated as spirits of the hills.

39.notes:
When its great round eyes light up, it sings a strange and soothing melody that lulls every listener into sleep. It draws breath deeply before the song, and its voice carries at the pitch that most invites drowsiness.
It puffs up in anger when its audience nods off, which is, of course, the constant fate of its concerts.

40.notes:
Its body is soft and rubbery, and its fine fur is counted among the most pleasant of textures. Angered, it draws in air and swells to an astonishing size.
Keepers warn that the swelling is not idle show, for a full Wigglytuff strikes with the whole weight of its body.

41.notes:
It forms colonies in perpetually dark places and finds its way by ultrasonic cries, having no eyes to speak of. Daylight sears its thin skin, and so it sleeps through the sun hanging from cave roofs.
It drinks the blood of living things, and travelers through the old tunnels carry torches as much against Zubat as against the dark.

42.notes:
Once it bites, it does not stop drinking until it grows too heavy to fly with grace. Its fangs are fine and hollow, and the bite is said to be scarcely felt.
It hunts the night sky of the caves and mountains, and a fat, low flying Golbat at dawn tells its own story.

43.notes:
By day it buries its face in the soil, and scholars long mistook it for a common weed. By night it wanders on its roots, sowing seeds as it goes.
It is drawn out by moonlight, and a field of walking Oddish under the moon is a sight travelers speak of ever after.

44.notes:
What oozes from its mouth is not drool but a nectar, sweet to smell at a distance and repulsive near, brewed to draw its prey. The great bud on its head drips with it.
The stench serves it as armor, and only one keeper in a hundred can stomach the creature at close quarters.

45.notes:
The larger its petals, the more toxic the pollen they carry, and its great head nods heavily with the weight of them. The bud opens with an audible burst.
It scatters clouds of allergenic pollen as it walks, and the wise pass a blooming Vileplume upwind.

46.notes:
It burrows to suck at tree roots, while the paired mushrooms on its back drink their nourishment from the bug that carries them. The mushrooms are prized in medicine.
Apothecaries pay well for the caps, which are said to lengthen life, and gathering them is a trade unto itself.

47.notes:
It keeps to dark and damp places, though scholars hold that this is the preference of the mushroom and not the bug beneath. The host is drained and the great cap does the thinking.
It is a sobering study, and the learned dispute to this day where the creature ends and the mushroom begins.

48.notes:
Its great eyes are in truth clusters of countless small ones, and by night its kind gathers wherever light burns. The fur sheds poison when it is seized.
It sees in darkness as clearly as noon, and it catches the small bugs that hide there.

49.notes:
The dust-like scales upon its wings are colored to their poisons, the dark bringing sickness and the pale bringing paralysis. It sheds them in a glittering cloud when it flaps in alarm.
It steals in by night to the light of lamps, and its wingbeats leave a shimmer of scales on the sill.

50.notes:
It lives about a yard beneath the ground, feeding on plant roots, and shows only its head above the tilled earth. Where it digs, the soil is left perfectly turned.
Farmers court its favor, for a field worked by Diglett needs neither plough nor spade.

51.notes:
A team of triplets sharing one burrow, whose digging is said to reach depths of sixty miles and to shake the very ground. They think as one and surface as one.
Where Dugtrio labors, earthquakes are blamed and forgiven in the same breath, for the turned earth is rich beyond price.

52.notes:
It adores round and shining things, and wanders the streets by night to gather dropped coins into a secret hoard. It walks with its charm held high.
It withdraws its claws in company and is soft footed as a shadow, but the hoard is defended in earnest.

53.notes:
Its fur has many admirers, yet it is a trying companion, fickle and proud, quick to scratch the hand that grooms it. It walks without sound on lithe muscle.
The jewel upon its brow gleams in lamplight, and it attacks in an instant when its patience thins.

54.notes:
It wears a vacant look while strange headaches gather in its skull, and when the ache peaks it looses powers of the mind it cannot afterward recall. It lulls its enemies with dullness.
Scholars watch it closely, for the sleepy duck is perhaps the least knowing wielder of the deepest arts.

55.notes:
It swims with an elegance that has been mistaken, at dusk, for the river spirits of old tales. When its brow glows it may move things without touching them.
It appears by the waterways at twilight, and boatmen leave a portion of their catch to keep its goodwill.

56.notes:
It is docile one moment and thrashing the next, for its anger arrives without warning or cause. In a rage it cannot tell friend from foe.
It lives in mountain troops whose quarrels echo down the valleys, and travelers give the noise a wide berth.

57.notes:
It is always furious, and tenacious besides, and it will not leave off a chase once begun though the quarry run for days. Even the glance of a stranger may set it off.
Yet its keepers note that in the instant of deepest rage its face grows strangely calm, and that is the moment most feared.

58.notes:
Very protective of its territory, it barks and bites to drive intruders from its ground. To its own keeper it is loyal beyond measure and fearless in defense.
It will not move a step while its keeper is behind it, and it has faced beasts thrice its size without flinching.

59.notes:
A beast admired since ancient times for its beauty, it runs as though on wings, and a day and a night of running is said to carry it six thousand miles. Its bark conveys such majesty that all who hear it bow.
The old paintings name it legendary, and though scholars quibble at the title, none who has seen it run disputes the spirit of it.

60.notes:
Its new legs are weak for running, and it plainly prefers to swim. The spiral upon its belly is in truth its innards showing through the thin skin, and the direction of the swirl differs by country.
The skin is slick and elastic, and many a hunting bird has lost its grip and its dinner together.

61.notes:
It lives with equal ease in water and on land, and when ashore it sweats to keep its body slick. The skin of its belly spiral is smooth where all else is moist.
Lulled by the slow turning of its own spiral, foes drop their guard, which the creature does not waste.

62.notes:
An adept swimmer at every stroke, it overtakes the best human swimmers with lazy ease, yet it makes its home on dry land. Its muscles never seem to tire.
It swims the cold straits for pleasure, and fishermen becalmed offshore have been towed home by a friendly one.

63.notes:
It reads the minds of those nearby, and sensing hostile intent it removes itself elsewhere before the intent becomes deed. It sleeps eighteen hours of every day, and teleports even in its dreams.
Catching one is a scholar's puzzle, for the net is read before it is thrown.

64.notes:
It emits peculiar alpha waves that bring headaches to any who linger near, and machines fail in its company. It holds a silver spoon that focuses its power.
It is written that a boy with strange gifts woke one morning transformed into this creature, though the learned call the tale a fable.

65.notes:
Its brain outperforms the finest calculating engines, and its wit is measured at five thousand by those who claim to measure such things. Its brain cells multiply until the day it dies, and it forgets nothing.
Its limbs wither as its mind swells, and it moves all it needs by thought alone, twin spoons in hand.

66.notes:
It loves above all to build its muscles, and it trains in every style of fighting art to grow stronger. It lifts a Graveler as a man lifts a sack of meal.
It is never satisfied with the day's training, and it seeks out stronger partners as other beasts seek food.

67.notes:
It carries heavy loads gladly, hardening its body with labor, and it does the work of many men wherever work is offered. Its strength wants a restraining belt to govern it.
At the docks and quarries it labors beside the workmen, and it is paid, quite contentedly, in its supper.

68.notes:
With four mighty arms it throws punches enough to send a foe clean over the horizon, or so the fighters' guild insists. It pins all four limbs of an opponent at once.
Its arms move faster than the eye at close work, though buttons and laces defeat the great fingers utterly.

69.notes:
A carnivorous plant that traps and eats bugs, drinking its water through root-like feet sunk in the soil. Rooted, it cannot flee, and so it spits a corroding fluid at whatever comes near.
It is planted like a garden row wherever it settles, and the hedgerows of it sway with no wind at all.

70.notes:
It hangs from branches by its hooked stem and takes unwary prey with a dousing of toxic powder. Though filled with acid it does not melt, for it oozes a neutralizing fluid besides.
When it hungers it swallows anything that moves beneath its bough, and digestion, the scholars note, is admirably swift.

71.notes:
It is said to live in great colonies deep in the jungles, from which, the records add plainly, no traveler has yet returned. It lures prey with a honeyed scent and melts it in its long mouth.
The vine it dangles twitches like a small creature, and that little lie has been the end of many.

72.notes:
It drifts in shallow seas, near invisible in the water, and anglers who hook it by accident are answered with stinging acid. Its body is mostly water, and it wilts like a dried leaf when beached.
By night its red orbs glow faintly, and a becalmed sea full of small lights is a warning every sailor knows.

73.notes:
Its tentacles are kept drawn in until the hunt, when all eighty are let out to weave a poisonous net about its prey. The red orbs upon its head flash when it is roused.
When the orbs glare across the swell, the fishing fleets turn for home and count the day well lost.

74.notes:
It is found on hillside and mountain paths, so like a boulder that people step upon it and are answered with swinging fists. It climbs steep ground hand over hand.
The longer it lives, the smoother its edges are worn, and the old ones sleep so soundly they are quarried by mistake.

75.notes:
It moves by rolling down slopes, over any obstacle in its path, without slowing and without complaint. Walking, it is slow and ungainly, and so it prefers the mountainside.
Where the rockfalls rumble at dusk, the quarrymen say the boulders are merely going home.

76.notes:
Its boulder body is hard beyond common stone and shrugs off blasting powder without a mark. Once a year it sheds its outer shell, and the cast-off husks are gathered as building stone.
It hurls itself from peak to peak by its own bursting force, and the mountain folk read the crashes like weather.

77.notes:
Its hooves are ten times harder than diamond, and whatever it tramples is flattened in short order. In the hour after birth its legs are weak, and it grows strong by chasing its parent.
The mane of fire does not burn a rider it trusts, which is the first lesson every stable hand learns by heart.

78.notes:
It is fiercely competitive and will chase anything that moves quickly, in the simple hope of a race. After a mere ten strides it reaches its full gallop, near a hundred and fifty miles in the hour.
At full speed the mane streams into pure flame, and watchers on the plain see only fire passing.

79.notes:
It is so absent of mind that it fails to notice its own tail being bitten, sometimes for the better part of a day. It fishes with that tail and forgets, more often than not, what it was doing.
Yet the learned say a great wisdom sleeps in its vacancy, and the lakeside shrines are raised to it in earnest.

80.notes:
A Shellder has fastened upon its tail and will not be parted, feeding on the host's leavings while the poison of its bite dulls what little pain the creature ever felt. It no longer notices much of anything.
The pair walk upright together on land, and philosophers argue whether the arrangement has one mind, or two, or none to speak of.

81.notes:
It hangs in the air by a force that undoes weight itself, appearing without warning wherever lightning gathers. It feeds upon the current of the great works and dams.
It is a made thing or a born thing, the scholars cannot settle which, and the creature offers no opinion.

82.notes:
Three Magnemite bound by a magnetism so strong it dries the very air around them. They appear in numbers when the sun is stormy with spots.
Where it passes, compasses spin and instruments lie, and the surveyors of the kingdom curse it by name.

83.notes:
The sprig of green it carries is its weapon, wielded much as a swordsman wields steel, and it will not be parted from a good stalk. In hard times it may eat the sprig, and then it goes at once in search of another.
It is choosy about its cuttings, and a duel between two over a fine stalk is a solemn thing to see.

84.notes:
A bird of two heads that makes up for poor flying with tremendous speed afoot, leaving prints deep enough to trip a traveler. The heads take their watches in turn.
The two heads are said to hold precisely opposite opinions in all matters, which does nothing to slow it down.

85.notes:
With three brains it lays complex plans, and while two heads sleep the third keeps the watch. If one head eats, all three are satisfied.
It runs the grasslands faster than most birds fly, and its tracks run straight as a surveyor's chain.

86.notes:
The horn upon its head is very hard and is used for breaking through thick ice from beneath. It sleeps by day in shallow water, nostrils closed against the sea.
It delights in bitter cold and grows listless in warm currents, and so it follows the ice the year around.

87.notes:
It stores the day's warmth in its body and swims a steady eight knots through seas cold enough to kill a man. Its long tail turns it as neatly as a rudder.
Sleeping on the ice by moonlight, it has been mistaken for a mermaid by more than one homesick sailor, and the error is recorded without shame.

88.notes:
It arises in filthy places and thrives by drinking the polluted sludge of drains and works. Where it passes, the germs it sheds let nothing grow.
It slips through any pipe or crack, and the town engineers know its routes better than their own maps.

89.notes:
It is covered thickly in a vile sludge so toxic that its very footprints poison the ground. A careless touch brings on a fever that wants bed rest.
It is banished from the towns by ordinance, and yet it drains the foulness from the waters it haunts, and the rivers run cleaner behind it.

90.notes:
Its shell turns aside every manner of attack, and only when the shell gapes is the creature at risk. By night it swims backward, opening and shutting the great valves.
Sand caught within the shell is turned by slow degrees into pearls, and divers court the risk for them.

91.notes:
When attacked it fires its horns in quick volleys, and what lies within the shell has never once been seen. In rough seas the spikes grow long and sharp.
It shuts against the tide and will not be pried, and the salvagers say a closed Cloyster keeps its secrets better than the sea keeps its drowned.

92.notes:
A creature of thin gas, near invisible, that wraps itself about the sleeping and the unwary. It can envelop a foe of any size.
It gutters like a candle in strong wind, and so it keeps to still air, old houses, and the windless hours.

93.notes:
It slips through stone walls as though they were mist, and for this it is said to have come from some other place entirely. Its tongue is made of gas, and its lick brings a trembling that does not soon stop.
It hunts in utter dark, and the lamplighters of the old towns were paid, in part, to keep it at the edge of the light.

94.notes:
Under a full moon it mimics the shadows of passersby and laughs at their fright, and the sudden chill of a warm night is said to be its greeting. It slips into a victim's own shadow and waits.
The scholars note, with some unease, that a shadow which moves a half step late is best not investigated.

95.notes:
It burrows through the earth at fifty miles in the hour, feeding on boulders as it goes, and the tunnels it leaves become the homes of Diglett. Its body grows smoother and darker with age.
The miners follow its old workings for the ore it exposes, and they leave the newest tunnels respectfully alone.

96.notes:
It sends its prey to sleep and then eats their dreams, sickening now and then on a nightmare. It remembers every dream it has ever eaten.
It prefers the dreams of children, which it holds tastier than those of the grown, and nurseries in its country burn a lamp against it.

97.notes:
It carries a pendulum always, swung at a steady rhythm that brings drowsiness to any who watch. It locks eyes before it works its arts.
There are records of children led away by its swinging charm, and the honest histories do not soften them.

98.notes:
Its pincers are weapons and balance both, and it walks its sideways walk along every tideline of the kingdom. If a pincer breaks, another grows in its place.
It bubbles at the mouth when roused, and the foam marks the sand like a line no rival crab should cross.

99.notes:
The great pincer holds a crushing force of ten thousand horsepower, or so the fishermen swear, yet its huge size makes it unwieldy to swing. The smaller claw does the finer work.
It raises the great claw to the sky when it postures, and the harbor children salute it back.

100.notes:
It is found near the great power works and is easily mistaken for a common ball, an error that has zapped generations of the incautious. It appeared, the records note, soon after the balls themselves were made.
What connection lies between the two, no scholar has settled, and the creature explodes when asked.

101.notes:
It stores its lightning under great pressure and bursts at small provocation, or at none. It feeds directly on the current of the works and grows fat before a storm.
The linesmen of the kingdom name it the blackout beast, and they say the lights of a whole town dim when one feeds.

102.notes:
Six eggs that are one creature, speaking each to each by a telepathy no other kind receives. They spin and cluster and are never parted far.
Cracked, an egg does not spill, and the six together are said to think as a single busy parliament.

103.notes:
Legend holds that on rare occasions one of its three heads drops off and goes its own way as a new cluster. The heads think separately and confer in murmurs.
It walks on long legs from grove to grove, and an orchard visited by night is left both robbed and planted.

104.notes:
It wears always the skull of its dead mother, and no living soul has seen its true face. It weeps on the night of the full moon, and the stains upon the skull are its tears.
The old books treat it gently, and so shall this one.

105.notes:
The bone it carries is its chief weapon, thrown skillfully as a boomerang and caught again without a glance. It has overcome its grief and grown fierce.
Somewhere in the world, the rumors say, lies a Marowak graveyard where the bones are gathered, though no map admits to it.

106.notes:
Its legs lengthen of themselves when it hurries, and it runs with long loping strides that eat the road. Kicking, it stretches farther still to catch a fleeing foe.
After battle it kneads its legs like a runner after a race, and the fighters' guild copies the habit devoutly.

107.notes:
Its twisting punches pulverize concrete, and the air itself is said to part before its fists. It rests, quite strictly, after three minutes of fighting.
Its blows move faster than sight, and the judges of the guild score its matches by sound alone.

108.notes:
Its tongue extends the length of two men and is nimbler than its hands, wielded for feeding, fighting, and cleaning alike. The lick leaves a tingling that is long remembered.
Whatever the tongue touches is remembered by taste, and it knows its keeper blindfolded among a hundred.

109.notes:
It stores several kinds of toxic gas in its swollen body and is prone to exploding without warning. The gases within are lighter than air, and so it drifts.
It hovers over middens and marshes, sipping foul air like wine, and its round face wears, at all times, a look of mild contentment.

110.notes:
Where two kinds of poison gas meet over long years, two Koffing may fuse into this doubled creature. The two heads breathe each other's fumes in turn.
Its inner gases, diluted to the highest degree, are made into the finest perfumes of the capital, a fact the perfumers do not advertise.

111.notes:
Its bones are a thousandfold harder than a man's, and it knocks wagons flying without breaking stride. It charges in one direction only, and turning is a project.
Its small brain holds a single thought at a time, and once it is running, the thought has already been forgotten.

112.notes:
Armored in hide like plate, it walks upright and wades in molten rock as a farmer wades a stream. The horn upon its snout bores through solid boulders.
Its hide turns cannon shot, say the old soldiers, and its brain woke only when it first stood on two legs.

113.notes:
A rare and gentle creature said to bring happiness to whoever wins its trust. It lays several eggs a day, so nourishing that the sick sit up after one spoonful.
It haunts the houses of healing of its own accord, and the nurses count one Chansey worth three of themselves, and say so.

114.notes:
Its whole body is swathed in wide blue vines, like seaweed grown ashore, and what lies beneath them no scholar has recorded. The vines shake gently as it walks.
It snares whatever moves within reach, though the captured report, somewhat sheepishly, that the grip mostly tickles.

115.notes:
The infant rides in its mother's belly pouch and rarely ventures out before its third year. In defense of the little one she will not yield though gravely wounded.
One does not pass between a Kangaskhan and her young, and the field guides print the warning in red.

116.notes:
From the water's surface it shoots down flying bugs with well aimed bursts of ink. Its broad fins beat quickly, and it can swim backward while facing forward.
When the current runs too strong it anchors by its curled tail to coral, and whole gardens of them sway together in the tide.

117.notes:
It swims backward with ease, sculling with wing-like fins and a stout tail, and its spines carry a poison worth respecting. The male, curiously, is the one that rears the young.
Its fins and bones are prized in medicine, and it is hunted for them, a fact the honest almanac must record.

118.notes:
Its tail fin billows like a gown in a ballroom, and it is called the Water Queen in every river town. It swims steadily against fast streams at five knots.
For all its finery it is a fighter, and its horn has taught many an angler the difference between pretty and tame.

119.notes:
In the spawning season it gathers from all the country round, and the rivers run a brilliant red with the crowding of it. The male dances then, and takes on his finest colors.
It bores nesting holes in riverbed stones with the horn upon its brow, and guards the eggs against all comers.

120.notes:
An enigmatic creature that grows back any limb it loses, so long as the glowing core at its center is whole. It gathers on the shore at nightfall.
By night the beaches wink with red cores like a second sky fallen, and the fishermen steer home by it.

121.notes:
Its core glows in the seven colors of the rainbow, and there are those who prize the core as a gem beyond price. Its body grows always toward perfect symmetry.
It is said to send strange signals from its core toward the night sky, and to whom it signals, no one can say.

122.notes:
Its fingertips harden the very air into an unseen wall, and it builds rooms and stairways where a passerby sees nothing at all. Interrupted in its miming, it slaps the offender with broad hands.
Once it has walled a road in jest, the wall must be walked around, for the creature will not unmake a good joke.

123.notes:
It moves with such speed that it seems to multiply, and its scythed forearms cut through logs at a stroke. In tall grass its colors hide it entirely.
The swordsmiths of the old school visit it in the meadows, it is said, to be reminded what an edge is.

124.notes:
It walks with a swaying rhythm that sets onlookers dancing whether they will or no. Its speech is near to human speech, though what it says is understood by no one.
The learned hold that its dancing is its language, and that the creature has been talking to us, patiently, all along.

125.notes:
It is found near the great power works, feeding on current, and when it wanders, whole towns go dark behind it. Its body crackles at all hours.
Before a storm the herds climb to high ground and call the lightning down upon themselves, and the hills flash white with their feasting.

126.notes:
Its body burns always with an orange glow, and among open flames it cannot be seen at all. Wounds are seared shut the moment they are taken.
It was found first at the mouths of volcanoes, and it breathes fire as easily as the rest of the world breathes air.

127.notes:
What its great horns seize is not released until it is crushed, and what cannot be crushed is swung about and thrown a good way. In cold seasons it hides deep in the woods.
It cannot abide the cold, and the first frost sends it to sleep in the deep timber until the world warms again.

128.notes:
It whips itself with its three tails to heighten its fury, then charges at full speed in a line that nothing much bends. It is not content unless it is charging.
The herdsmen of the plains rank a season by its stampedes, and their fences by what survives them.

129.notes:
A feeble and pathetic fish, famous across the kingdom for being of no use whatever, that leaps and splashes for no reason and is caught mid-leap by every passing bird. In the distant past, the records insist, it was somewhat stronger.
And yet the patient keeper is repaid a thousandfold, as the next entry will attest.

130.notes:
Huge and vicious, it is capable of unmaking a whole city in a rage, and once it appears it does not calm until all about it is leveled. The old chronicles blame whole famines upon its passing.
That so terrible a dragon rises from so wretched a fish is the kingdom's favorite sermon, and its truest one.

131.notes:
A gentle giant of the sea that ferries travelers across the water on its back, singing softly when the crossing pleases it. It understands human speech.
It was hunted near to nothing in the old days, and every crossing it grants is counted a forgiveness.

132.notes:
It rewrites its own substance to become a perfect copy of whatever stands before it, faults and all. Made to laugh, it cannot hold the disguise.
When two of them meet, each tries to become the other, and the philosophers have not yet recovered.

133.notes:
Its nature is unsettled and unwritten, and it may become any of several creatures as its surroundings decide. Its blood, the scholars say, is a question waiting to be asked.
Keepers prize it beyond most beasts, for in one small body sleep many possible futures.

134.notes:
Its cells are kin to water itself, and in the shallows it fades from sight altogether. The finned tail has been taken for a mermaid's more than once.
It loves clean shores, and its arrival at a beach is taken as the water's own testimony.

135.notes:
It drinks the charge of the very air, and every hair upon it stands like a spearpoint when the storm gathers. It looses bolts of ten thousand volts.
It is prickly in temper as in coat, and its moods change with the weather, which is to say, constantly.

136.notes:
It stores the heat of its meals in an inner flame sac, and its body burns at sixteen hundred degrees when roused. It fluffs its collar of fur to cool itself.
It sleeps by the hearth like a hound, and in the cold uplands a household with a Flareon burns no other fuel.

137.notes:
A made creature, built entirely of written code, that moves through the unseen rooms of the calculating engines as a fish moves through water. It was the first of its kind in the world.
It neither breathes nor hungers, and the scribes of this codex confess they do not know what page it belongs to, and record it anyway.

138.notes:
Long extinct, it is called back to life in rare cases from the spiral fossils of the old sea floor. It sculled the ancient waters with ten twisting limbs.
Revived, it paddles the modern shallows amiably enough, ten thousand lifetimes from home.

139.notes:
A hunter of the ancient seas whose heavy shell, the scholars judge, at last made prey too swift for it. What its coils took, they did not release.
It died out once already, the records note, and it carries the fact about with it, in stone.

140.notes:
It was raised from a fossil of the old ocean floor, and on rare occasions it is found living still, unchanged in three hundred million years. It hides upon the seabed under its hard dome.
The eyes upon its back glow faintly in the dark water, and the divers who meet that gaze report it steady and entirely unimpressed.

141.notes:
Its sleek shape was made for swimming fast in the old seas, and its scythed arms slash prey and drain it. In time, the scholars say, it crawled ashore to hunt.
Its silhouette against the shallows is the oldest shape in this codex, and it has not softened with the years.

142.notes:
A ferocious flyer of the ancient skies, restored from old amber, that goes for the throat with serrated fangs and shrieks high enough to crack glass. The modern sky puzzles it.
It circles the peaks looking for an age that has ended, and its cry at dusk is the loneliest sound in the mountains.

143.notes:
It eats near nine hundred pounds in a day and then sleeps where it stops, and children play safely upon its great belly. It is not finicky, and things eaten off the ground digest without complaint.
When one lies down across a mountain road, the road is closed, and the kingdom has learned to wait.

144.notes:
A legendary bird of ice that is said to appear to doomed travelers lost in the snows. It chills the moisture of the air into snow as it flies.
Whether it comes as omen or as mercy, the accounts do not agree, and those best placed to say did not return to say it.

145.notes:
A legendary bird of lightning that appears from parting thunderclouds, dropping enormous bolts as it goes. Its feathers crackle and snap when it shakes them.
It is said to dwell where the storms are born, and the power works post a watchman against its visits.

146.notes:
The legendary bird of fire, whose every wingbeat is a flash of flame against the sky. It is said to bring an early spring to the wintry lands it crosses.
The hurt and the weary, the tales hold, may dip themselves in the magma of its mountain and rise mended, though the tales are quiet on the details.

147.notes:
Long held a myth, until a small colony was found living beneath the water of a deep lake. It sheds its skin again and again as the life within it swells.
The shed skins wash ashore like pale silk, and the lake folk gather them and say nothing to visitors.

148.notes:
A mystical serpent trailing a gentle air about it, said to change the weather with the light of its crystal orbs. The lakes it haunts are calm out of season.
Farmers of the dry valleys keep its image over the door, and in drought years the offerings at the lakeside grow generous.

149.notes:
For all its bulk it circles the globe, they say, in sixteen hours, and it flies over raging seas without trouble. Its wit is said to match a man's.
Sailors tell of ships steered through storms by its guiding, and of a dragon that carries the drowning to shore, and the telling does not vary much from port to port.

150.notes:
It was made by human hands, after years of terrible grafting and tampering upon the blood of Mew. The body was given every power, and the makers, the records admit, forgot to give it a gentle heart.
It lies still in the deep cave to husband its strength, and thinks, and what it thinks about its makers is its own affair.
150.scribe: The only creature in this codex that men must answer for.

151.notes:
So rare that many experts call it a mirage, it is said to show itself only to those pure of heart who greatly wish to see it. Within its blood sleep the codes of every creature in this codex, and it can work any art it pleases.
It makes itself unseen at will, and passes through the world unnoticed, which is perhaps the kindest reading of why so few have found it.
151.scribe: A persistent rumor places one beneath a lorry by the great ship at Vermilion's docks. The scribes have moved the lorry. There was nothing.
